In this work, we study supervised fine-tuning (SFT) by pretraining transformers on a controlled context-free grammar with hierarchical latent structure, the Random Hierarchy Model (RHM), and fine-tuning with a restricted subset of its generative rules. While during pretraining the model's ability to generate with the correct grammar rules coincides with building the internal representations of the corresponding latent, we find that SFT exhibits a very different dynamics: (i) the generation of deleted rules changes on a fast timescale inversely proportional to the magnitude of the token-latent correlation; meanwhile, their corresponding representations stay intact; (ii) the hidden representations of the deleted rules become forgotten on a much longer timescale, associated with a slow drift of the network parameters. Finally, we observe analogous results in a realistic setup with natural language, suggesting that this timescale separation in forgetting is a more general phenomenon of fine-tuning language models.

papers.title: Certify What You Plant: Shortcut-Free Proof Depth in Logical Reasoning Data
papers.abstract: Procedurally generated logic problems are used to both evaluate and train reasoning in language models. Their difficulty is usually set by planting a proof, that is, by sampling a proof of the desired depth and stating its premises as the problem. However, a planted proof is only one possible proof. A problem can also have shorter proofs, or several unrelated ones, and its stated depth then overstates what solving it requires. We measure what a problem actually requires, relative to a stated set of inference rules. For each problem, we compute the steps every proof must make, the shortest proof, the number of minimal proofs and the indispensable premises, and export certificates that an independent checker verifies. Audits of eight datasets find depth that is forced (ProofWriter, Blocksworld), problems labelled depth 5 that require about two specific rule applications (FLDx2), and answers that need no particular step (ZebraLogic). We then construct problems whose every proof has a requested structure, using a catalog of shortcuts proved once per rule set. Every constructed problem is checked in full and comes with its own certificate. In training, the best data mixes depths and problem types. At equal size, such mixtures of certified problem types, including model-checking problems that forward generation does not produce, transfer better than FLDx2-style derivation data for Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 8B.

papers.title: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis in Jacobian-Space: Language and Vision Models Agree Approximately Up to a Rotation
papers.abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) posits that AI models converge toward a shared representation of the world, even when trained on different data modalities. Previous work has found evidence for the PRH in the activations of vision and language models. In this work, we ask whether vision and language models also converge in how they act on these representations: precisely, in how these internal representations affect the models' output. At a chosen layer of a transformer, the Jacobian lens gives every word in the vocabulary (or class in an image classifier) a vector in the hidden state: the vector that most increases the model's tendency to generate that word, at that position or later, or to predict that class. Collectively, these vectors make up what is referred to as the model's J-space. We find evidence of the PRH in J-space across vision and language models, and furthermore, we find that J-spaces mostly converge up to a rotation. That is, a single rotation, fitted on a subset of words, approximately maps one model's J-space onto another's, and so applies to words and classes it was not fitted on. A word's vector, rotated from a text-only language model's J-space into the visual patch tokens of a vision-language model, changes the object the vision-language model says is in the image (and only in the image region where it is added). Rotated into an image generator's text conditioning, a word's vector changes the object in the generated image. Rotated into an ImageNet classifier (trained without text), it raises that object's class score above almost all others, and vice versa. This suggests that models converge not only in how they represent the world, but also in how they act on it.

papers.title: Fuel-Efficient Formation Flying via Constrained Extremum Seeking
papers.abstract: This paper presents a model-free autonomous guidance architecture for minimal drag of a trailing aircraft in formation flight. Realizing the fuel savings resulting from such a formation requires learning and tracking a time-varying vortex while avoiding locations where the aircraft experiences an abrupt rolling moment disturbance. A guidance architecture for fuel-efficient safe flight, called Adaptive Plateau-seeking Optimal Guidance with ModulatEd Excitations (APOGEE), is proposed herein. Key features of APOGEE are its ability to modulate the amplitude of the excitation required to learn the unknown objective and constraint functions, to adaptively adjust the learning rates, and to keep the flight safe during the search for the optimal formation. A threshold-gated modulation reduces the amplitude of excitation when the objective function reaches an acceptably large value, thus improving flying qualities and further reducing fuel consumption. Furthermore, a Newton-based learning rule, whose estimate of the inverse of the Hessian is spectrally clamped, adapts the learning rates to the local curvature of the objective function in order to accelerate convergence and lower the chance of overshooting the optimum. Finally, a safety filter having an unknown constraint function is used to prevent a loss of control event prompted by the above mentioned disturbance. The efficacy of APOGEE is demonstrated by using a high-fidelity model of an F-16 jet and an experimentally obtained vortex model. Being model-free, APOGEE does not require modeling the dependence of the unknown functions on the characteristics of the leading aircraft, the flight condition, the crosswind, and the vortex-induced turbulence.

papers.title: Bosonic Magic Resources at Quantum Criticality
papers.abstract: Non-Gaussianity is a resource for bosonic quantum information processing, providing a necessary ingredient for universal quantum computation in continuous-variable systems. Here we quantify non-Gaussianity in the ground state of the one-dimensional extended Bose-Hubbard model using quantum relative entropy (QRE), a measure determined solely by one-body correlations. The scaling of the QRE with system size reveals quantum phase transitions involving hidden and conventional order. We connect QRE scaling in the weakly interacting superfluid phase to Luttinger-liquid correlations and identify distinct critical signatures in its extensive and subleading contributions. At the Mott-Haldane transition, subtracting the extensive background reveals a pronounced peak in the subleading contribution, providing a clear signature of the onset of hidden string order. At the Haldane-density-wave transition, the extensive contribution to the QRE instead exhibits scaling consistent with Ising criticality. These results establish non-Gaussianity as a probe of many-body criticality, linking bosonic quantum resources to strongly correlated matter.

papers.title: Lost in Translation, Not in Confidence: Benchmarking and Calibrating Multilingual Decision Models
papers.abstract: Decision models are language models fine-tuned to return a probability for each option of a typed query, which routers and guardrails threshold directly. They are built on multilingual bases but ranked almost entirely in English. We evaluate 25 top-ranked open-weight decision models on 17 tasks in 14 languages, comparing each language with English on parallel items. Every model loses accuracy in every language, from about 2 points in high-resource languages to 8 in Tamil, while confidence falls only half as much: a threshold set for 95\% accuracy in English yields 90% in Tamil. The size of the loss is set by the language and the base model rather than by leaderboard rank. In 81 controlled fine-tuning runs, task skill learned in English transfers to other languages and a few thousand target-language items narrow large losses, but neither more data nor full-parameter tuning closes them. Finally, the same test items are answered more accurately in all 23 benchmark--language pairs we compare when an LLM rather than a person translated them, so LLM-translated test sets understate the gap.

papers.title: Change Partners at Every Layer: Balanced Random Regrouping for Model Merging
papers.abstract: Model merging combines fine-tuned experts into one model that serves many tasks without retraining, but merging many experts this way substantially reduces accuracy. Grouping offers a middle ground: at every layer or weight matrix, the $N$ experts are divided into $K<N$ groups, the experts in a group are merged into one shared module, and a task uses the module merged from its expert's group. Natural choices are to keep the same partners across layers or to group similar experts. Surprisingly, we find that randomly changing partners at every layer outperforms both. We call this Balanced Random Regrouping (BRR): it independently partitions the experts into $K$ equal-sized random groups at each layer (BRR-layer) or weight matrix (BRR-matrix) and merges each group with an existing method. With validation-selected merge scales, both BRR variants outperform reusing one grouping across layers in all 24 CLIP settings, by 1.0-6.8 points, and BRR-matrix also outperforms the similarity-based FlexMerge in every setting. A first-order analysis explains this gain. At each layer, merging a task's expert with its partners shifts the task's output features; when the partners are the same at every layer, these shifts tend to point in similar directions and add up, whereas with new partners at every layer they vary independently and add up less on average. A series of experiments supports this analysis, which further guides a grouping search that can outperform BRR.

papers.title: NeuroRefine: Six-Head MLP Content Conditioning and Qwen Refinement for Faithful fMRI Decoding
papers.abstract: Reconstructing seen images from fMRI has advanced through diffusion models, but the current state-of-the-art Brain-IT pipeline still has a lossy bottleneck: its low-level branch outlines the figure well, yet the diffusion model that follows frequently mispaints colour, object identity and layout. We move one step backward and condition the refiner directly on the fMRI-derived low-level image, using six one-hidden-layer MLP heads (scene, main-subject category, count, colour, object, layout) to predict the content prompt that guides a frozen Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 model. On the 930 shared NSD concepts, scored with Brain-IT's own metric code on the same ground truth, NeuroRefine reaches a CLIP image cosine of 0.755 against 0.735 for Brain-IT enhanced and produces markedly sharper images, while the saturated 2-way identification is unchanged. The low-level image supplies an explicit spatial prior rather than a lossless layout: refinement trades some layout agreement (0.541 against 0.638) for semantic fidelity and texture. We then show that the standard panel is multi-factor: a high PixCorr can coexist with completely different content, so we read the low-level and semantic factors separately and quantify where they disagree. Finally, we trace the cortical sources of the prompt heads across subjects and report their causal lesion profile and the fMRI noise ceiling. Direction errors are left to future work.

papers.title: Nonzero central quotients of the Virasoro enveloping algebra are simple
papers.abstract: We prove a conjecture of Petukhov and Sierra that the central quotient $\mathrm{U}(\mathrm{Vir})/(z-c)$ of the universal enveloping algebra of the Virasoro algebra is simple for all $c \neq 0$. We extend the result to the $N=1$ super-Virasoro algebras. Our proof reveals a new connection between enveloping algebras and polynomial identity algebras. Although the enveloping algebra itself does not satisfy a polynomial identity, the adjoint action on each filtered piece does satisfy a standard identity. In particular, the Witt algebra $W$, as an adjoint module over itself, satisfies the standard identity $\mathrm{St}_4$, whereas $\mathrm{Vir}$ fails by a nonzero multiple of the central charge. Propagating this gap through the PBW filtration of $\mathrm{U}(\mathrm{Vir})/(z-c)$, for every nonscalar element, we construct an alternating adjoint operator that lowers its order by exactly one. As applications, we compute the annihilators of all representations with nonzero central character, prove a strengthened form of Etingof's conjecture on nonsplit extensions of $W$-modules, and reduce the classification of prime ideals of $\mathrm{U}(\mathrm{Vir})$ to those of $\mathrm{U}(W)$.

papers.title: Machine Learning for Calabi--Yau Geometry and Heterotic Compactification
papers.abstract: Quantitative predictions from string compactification depend on geometric data that are difficult to compute analytically. This review surveys machine learning approaches to predicting topological properties of Calabi-Yau manifolds, discusses the search for new Calabi-Yau fourfolds, as well as numerical methods for approximating Ricci-flat metrics. In the context of heterotic compactifications, we explain how bundle metrics and harmonic matter forms enter calculations of canonically normalized Yukawa couplings and axion-matter interactions. We also outline applications to flux compactifications, warped and corrected backgrounds, and geometric structures beyond the Calabi-Yau setting. Finally, we review available datasets and software, highlight connections with analytic methods, and discuss geometric constraints, numerical validation, and recent progress in rigorous error control.

papers.title: Gauge symmetry permits extremely low-depth random unitary circuits
papers.abstract: Continuous global symmetries can obstruct logarithmic-depth symmetric unitary $k$-designs and pseudorandom unitaries (PRUs) through long-range correlations. We ask whether gauge symmetries impose analogous limitations. For $\mathrm{U}(1)$ lattice gauge theories, we identify a randomization scale $c$, the minimum patch size needed for matter to screen every allowed boundary-flux mismatch, and a diffusive scale governing boundary-flux correlations. Glued circuits built from gauge-symmetric unitaries with subdiffusive support are efficiently distinguishable from gauge-symmetric Haar-random unitaries, whereas local controlled designs can be glued into global approximate designs when overlaps exceed the diffusive scale multiplied by a logarithmic factor. Our analysis suggests incomplete screening limits design guarantees to constant order, whereas strictly locally random systems with complete local screening ($c=1$) admit a local tensor-product description, permitting superpolynomial design orders and logarithmic-depth designs and PRUs. We construct a toy model of charged black-hole evaporation in which insufficient screening makes uninterrupted complete discharge exponentially unlikely in $c$, whereas strict local randomization removes this screening obstruction. This motivates a quantum-information analogue of the weak gravity conjecture, requiring the available charged spectrum to support complete local screening in addition to superextremality. We conjecture that this condition allows gauge-symmetric systems to scramble as rapidly as unconstrained ones and support this by constructing logarithmic-depth approximate strong designs and strong PRUs.

papers.title: Multisensory Hybrid TV
papers.abstract: Traditional TV media content exclusively involves audiovisual streams. Multi-sensorial media (mulsemedia) introduces sensory effects such as ambient lighting, vibration, scents, wind, or temperature to stimulate other senses and create more enjoyable, realistic, and immersive content consumption experiences. This paper presents an MPEG-V- and HbbTV-based end-to-end solution for providing multi-sensorial hybrid (broadcast/broadband) TV content consumption experiences. A prototype following the proposal has been implemented on an end-to-end HbbTV-compliant platform, including both video streams and sensory effects metadata delivery and synchronous consumption, replicating a mulsemedia hybrid TV service. The prototype has been subjectively evaluated and validated by 106 participants with diverse profiles, yielding highly satisfactory results, including overall enjoyment, realism, immersion, perceived synchronization, and QoE enhancement. Furthermore, the results have also revealed interesting demographic patterns, such as participants with higher academic levels reporting lower satisfaction scores in general, distinct gender-based preferences regarding sensory acceptance, and potential barriers to commercial adoption, where higher realism and immersion do not translate into an equivalent willingness to pay for these enhanced TV services.

papers.title: Building a Unified Inline Code Editing Model for GitHub Copilot
papers.abstract: AI-assisted coding ranges from fully agentic coding to inline code suggestions in the editor. Inline suggestions require predicting a developer's most likely next edit from an editing session. The next edit may lie at the cursor, in nearby lines, or farther away, and one editing intent can span several of these. The preceding system queries separate completion, nearby edit, and long-distance edit models, each with its own output format, in a fixed sequence; it thus cannot express intents spanning distant locations in one response, can require several sequential model calls per suggestion, and prioritizes completion even when a correction would serve better. We present a unified model that predicts all three edit types in one output space: a sequence of anchored diff patches specifying locations, deleted lines, and added lines. This representation permits multiple edits per response, so the client can serve later edits from a cache without further model calls. We train this model in two phases, first unifying next edit and long-distance edit prediction, then adding code completion. We synthesize multi-edit supervision from single-edit data via model pseudolabeling and edit history playback. We use a binary LLM-graded reward, a patch validity taxonomy shared by data filtering, reward, and evaluation, and grader boosting for targeted failure modes. Phase 2 also adapts how the client processes and presents model outputs. In controlled online A/B experiments in GitHub Copilot, Phase 1 significantly reduces time to display by 6.77% and output tokens by 58.93% relative to the three-model baseline. In Phase 2, the 3-in-1 model and client adaptations reduce dismissed suggestions per user by 10.06% relative to the 2-in-1 model paired with the completion model. Throughout this report, we also share our methodology and learnings in evaluation, training, and end-to-end model and system design.

papers.title: Large-scale Model Merging via Recovery-aware Task Weighting
papers.abstract: Model merging combines multiple task-specific expert models into a single model. However, merging preserves expert capabilities unevenly across tasks. This imbalance is particularly pronounced in large-scale settings, where some tasks can suffer severe capability losses even when average accuracy remains high. To address this imbalance, we introduce Recovery-aware Task Weighting (RaTW), a model merging framework that assigns larger weights to tasks whose expert capabilities are poorly retained by an initial merged model. We quantify these recovery opportunities as the fraction of a task's labeled validation samples that its expert predicts correctly but the initial merged model gets wrong, and use the resulting task weights to re-merge the experts. To evaluate merging at large scale, we construct CLIPMerge-100, a 100-task benchmark with task-specific experts on CLIP ViT-L/14 and ViT-B/32. Across eleven merging methods with 20, 50, and 100 tasks on two CLIP backbones, RaTW improves both mean accuracy and tail20 (the mean expert-normalized accuracy of the 20% worst-retained tasks) in all 33 ViT-L/14 settings and 32 of 33 ViT-B/32 settings. We further introduce ReForge++, which combines RaTW with iterative model refinement and outperforms all evaluated baselines, including a matched-budget control, in both mean accuracy and tail20 across all settings.

papers.title: What Does RL Post-Training Teach Text-to-Image Models? A Skill-Wise Analysis of Flow-GRPO
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training has become a standard way to improve text-to-image flow models: Flow-GRPO lifts the GenEval score of SD3.5-M from 0.63 to 0.95, a gain read as the model having learned compositional generation. We ask how much of that gain the base model's own samples already contained, by measuring pass@k over shared noise seeds, one skill at a time, before and after RL, on prompts never used in training. The answer differs by skill. On four of GenEval's six skills, where 32 base samples already solve almost every prompt, the gain is sharpening: one post-trained sample is worth 4 to 10 base samples, and pass@32 barely moves. On spatial relations it is unlocking: pass@32 rises from 0.69 to 1.00, 128 base samples do not match one post-trained sample, and prompts the base model never solved in 32 samples are solved 93% of the time, as often as those it solved. The benchmark average, 31 base samples per post-trained sample, describes no skill. Relations carry 35% of the gain; of the other 65%, selecting among 8 base samples with the judge behind the reward recovers nine tenths. We propose an account of when each occurs: within a prompt, a group-relative update re-weights only the outcomes its samples contain, and a flow policy cannot widen the noise that produces them; across prompts, shared parameters let successes on some prompts repair a deficit common to many. The same anatomy applies to a text-rendering checkpoint. The account's predictions are tested with a checkpoint trained without KL, within-prompt diversity, and controlled training that holds object classes out, where sharpening comes first and transfers, and unlocking follows, on practised objects before unseen ones.

papers.title: When does a noisy Bell pair attain the Rains bound?
papers.abstract: Two entangled Bell-diagonal qubit states with the same singlet fraction have the same Rains bound. We prove that their attainable rates under operations preserving the positive partial transpose can nevertheless differ: the bound is attained if and only if one of the Bell probabilities vanishes. Every mixed entangled isotropic state, in every finite dimension, lies strictly below its bound. This refutes the attainment suggested by finite-block numerics, and places the two-way quantum capacity of the qubit depolarizing channel strictly below its relative-entropy bound.

papers.title: What Must LLM Agents Communicate? From Information Loss to Communication Failures
papers.abstract: When evidence is distributed across LLM agents, a team may collectively possess all the information needed for a decision yet fail to use it effectively. What must agents communicate for accurate joint predictions, and when does interaction help? We study three requirements for effective communication: sufficiency of the information conveyed, selection of relevant evidence, and utilization of received information. Drawing on information theory and communication complexity, we develop a framework that combines theoretical benchmarks with controlled experiments and message-level analyses. We find that local probability reports can discard essential information, with theoretical information loss closely matching observed performance penalties. Query-first interaction improves predictions when relevant evidence depends on a private query, but compact one-shot representations can eliminate this advantage. Even when sufficient information is communicated, agents may fail to select or use it correctly. Together, these findings distinguish fundamental communication limits from failures in how LLM agents communicate and use information.

papers.title: A Tale of Two Type IIb Supernovae: Radio-loud and Radio-silent Candidate Counterparts to Sub-solar Mass Gravitational-wave Triggers
papers.abstract: On 2025 November 12, the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration reported S251112cm, a gravitational-wave (GW) candidate from a compact binary merger with at least one sub-solar-mass component. Optical follow-up identified SN 2025adtq, a Type IIb supernova (SN) within the localization volume that exploded a few days before the merger. SN 2025adtq is the second Type IIb SN found to be potentially coincident with a sub-solar-mass GW candidate, after SN 2025ulz (S250818k). A key question is whether such SNe harbor fast, possibly collimated ejecta from a central engine, as invoked in ``superkilonova'' scenarios for forming sub-solar-mass neutron stars. We present deep Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array observations of SN 2025adtq from the JAGWAR program, spanning 139-216 days after the GW trigger at 6-10 GHz. The radio properties of SN 2025adtq differ substantially from those of SN 2025ulz: whereas SN 2025ulz has a significant 6-10 GHz counterpart, SN 2025adtq remains undetected to 3sigma limits of ~7.8 uJy, implying a radio luminosity density one order of magnitude below that of SN 2025ulz at a comparable epoch, excluding jet models that remained viable for SN 2025ulz. This diversity in radio properties calls for systematic multi-wavelength follow up observations of candidate sub-solar events in future runs of the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA detectors.

papers.title: The Transverse Finiteness Conjecture for pseudo-Anosov flows via universal circles
papers.abstract: We prove Mosher's Transverse Finiteness Conjecture, posed in 1996. This states that every taut, finite depth foliation $\mathcal F$ of an atoroidal 3-manifold is almost transverse to at most finitely many pseudo-Anosov flows, up to orbit equivalence. Our strategy is to organize the flows that are almost transverse to $\mathcal F$ using their associated universal circles. This technique also establishes the following rigidity result: if a finite depth foliation $\mathcal F$ is almost transverse to a pseudo-Anosov flow $\varphi$ without perfect fits, then $\varphi$ is the unique pseudo-Anosov flow that is almost transverse to $\mathcal F$, up to orbit equivalence. In fact, in this setting, $\mathcal F$ has only one minimal universal circle.

papers.title: Kovács Vanishing for Excellent Log Canonical Threefolds
papers.abstract: We prove a vanishing theorem of S. Kovács for excellent log canonical threefolds whose closed points have perfect residue fields of sufficiently large characteristic. This vanishing theorem roughly says that LC threefold pairs are not far from being rational pairs (in the sense of Kollár \& Kovács and Schwede \& Takagi) if one includes a correction term. We apply this vanishing to prove a depth relation of Chou and resolution-invariance of cohomologies of ``essential divisors" for isolated log canonical threefolds in large characteristic, extending works of Ishii and Fujino. Using examples constructed by Bernasconi and Cascini-Tanaka, we show that these results fail in low characteristic. Finally, we show Kovács and Alexeev-Hacon's result (in char 0) that ``Irrational centers are LC centers" fails in every positive characteristic.

papers.title: Brand Recall and Category Accuracy in Language Models: An Audit of 1,000 B2B SaaS Brands
papers.abstract: A language model can name a brand without classifying it correctly. This study measures these outcomes separately for 1,000 B2B SaaS brands across 333 product categories. On Gemma 4 12B, with no external retrieval, category prompts elicit 510 brands (51.0%). A separate five-candidate category probe ranks the reference label first for 787 brands, a distractor first for 194, and yields little separation for 19. Among the 981 separated rankings, the error rate is 19.8%. It falls to 3.5% for the 547 brands with a winner-to-runner-up log-probability margin above 0.6. These are within-cohort measurements, not calibrated confidence estimates. Exploratory regressions associate technical coverage with recall and an owned-properties composite with category accuracy, but the composites use different adjustment sets and do not establish causal effects. Across four Gemma generations, measured recall is 39.8%, 44.3%, 51.1% and 51.0%. A separate representation-based sentiment measure has little linear association with customer ratings (r=0.03, n=921). The findings support reporting recall and category accuracy separately. Failure to elicit a brand does not establish its absence from model parameters or training data.

papers.title: StyleID++: Position-Decoupled and Structure-Coherent Style Retrieval across Diffusion Architectures
papers.abstract: Attention injection offers a remarkably simple route to training-free style transfer: content queries retrieve style keys and values inside a pretrained diffusion model. We show that this operation also creates an overlooked failure mode. Position signals that are useful within one image become a spurious shared coordinate system across two spatially unrelated images, causing content tokens to favor style tokens at similar coordinates. This cross-image positional leakage appears in both convolutional U-Nets and diffusion transformers (DiTs), despite their different position mechanisms. Removing the positional shortcut exposes a second problem: unconstrained global retrieval lets related content tokens select incompatible style regions, producing fragmented appearance. We present StyleID++, a training-free framework that addresses the two problems jointly. Position-Decoupled Retrieval reduces coordinate-dependent matching through circular padding in U-Nets and injection-only RoPE removal in DiTs, while preserving native position modeling elsewhere. Affinity-Coherent Refinement then regularizes style assignments with the content self-attention graph, encouraging structurally related tokens to retrieve compatible style evidence. We quantify the leakage with a coordinate--centroid correlation and a permutation test on the style reference. The permutation error can be driven to zero in both backbones, which identifies the position mechanism as the carrier of the leakage, and StyleID++ obtains the best ArtFID of all methods we compare.

papers.title: NuSrcAgent: An AI Agent for High-Energy Neutrino Source Searches
papers.abstract: Identifying the sources of high-energy cosmic neutrinos is crucial for understanding cosmic particle accelerators and probing new physics. IceCube provides public data that allow researchers to search independently for neutrino sources, but these analyses require substantial technical expertise and careful scientific choices. We present \system, the first publicly available AI agent for high-energy neutrino source searches. Compared to public likelihood codes, \system is easier to install and use, and supports more analysis types. To start an analysis, users need only specify a source or catalog. The agent takes natural-language requests, runs likelihood analyses on public IceCube event data, and saves the settings and calculation records so users can repeat the analyses. We demonstrate \system through single-source and catalog stacking analyses, obtaining results consistent with IceCube results. These examples also show its ability to search the literature, analyze non-power-law spectra using user-provided model code, and develop new analysis functions, such as signal-injection simulations. \system is also a powerful tool for improving and testing existing analysis code, as we demonstrate by using it to refine the background probability density functions and reduce residuals and spurious signal contributions in stacking analyses. \system makes high-energy neutrino data analysis more accessible to the broader research community. Code and usage instructions: \href{https://github.com/beizhouphys/NuSrcAgent}{\faGithub\ {\tt github.com/beizhouphys/NuSrcAgent}}.

papers.title: Sparse Adaptation for In-Context Learning on Data Streams
papers.abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) generates massive data streams, making edge computing essential for low-latency applications and 5G networks. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) enable adaptation through in-context examples rather than parameter updates, but evolving streams challenge context relevance and computational efficiency. This work introduces SAIL, a framework for sparse adaptation of TFMs that reuses the model's key--value cache between adaptation events. SAIL reconstructs its support set only when drifts in stream structure indicate potential context inadequacy, while the structural representation itself is updated by changes in predictive performance. SAIL combines prequential error monitoring with online, class-specific micro-clustering to detect changes in cluster mass, class separability, and feature-space coverage. Upon adaptation, a context budget is allocated proportionally to class mass, and the most recently updated micro-clusters provide representative observations for refitting. This limits context redundancy and computational cost while preserving recent structural information.

papers.title: Beyond the blur: Radial binning trumps stellar migration in resolved star formation histories
papers.abstract: Spatially resolved galaxy properties are routinely derived from integral-field spectroscopy and increasingly from multi-band photometry as a wealth of photometric data become available in large surveys like LSST/Rubin. Spatially resolved star formation histories (SFHs) offer a detailed view of galaxy growth and quenching by tracing the timing and location of star formation within a galaxy up to one billion years in the past. However, stellar migration between spaxels may strongly bias these reconstructions. Quantifying this bias remains challenging as few Milky-Way mass simulations fully resolve initial stellar dispersions or migration rates. We use the well-validated h277 Milky-Way-mass cosmological zoom simulation, which resolves both via explicitly tying star formation to the non-equilibrium abundance of H2, to assess the quality of specific star formation rates (sSFR) radial profiles inferred from resolved SFHs against actual values from stellar particle tracking. Across several evolutionary windows spanning a range of stellar activity stages from quiescent to star-bursting, we find that the adaptive radial binning imposed by S/N constraints in photometric SED fitting actually mitigates most of the blurring/mixing effects of stellar migration on inferred radial profiles up to lookback times of 1.5 Gyr. This allows for proper recovery of not only the average sSFR but also its radial slope, its relative changes in scatter across radial annuli and even approximate localization of low-z star-forming clumps. Only galaxies having undergone a major merger across the considered lookback time display discrepant, unreliable sSFR profiles, hence should not be considered for such reconstructions.

papers.title: Who Attributes a Mind to Whom? Mutual Theory of Mind in Simulated User-Assistant Conversation
papers.abstract: When users assume that an AI chatbot has mental states, they are more likely to develop over-reliance, emotional dependence, and in extreme cases, psychological harm or self-harm. However, how these mind attributions arise in conversations and how human or AI factors influence this is still unknown. We study how users attribute minds using a minimal framework: a simulated user with different characteristics chats with assistants that differ in social style and memory. We also introduce a message-level measure of who attributes a mind to whom in four directions, checked with trained coders and applied by a fine-tuned encoder that reproduces an LLM judge. Our results show that, on average, nine out of thirteen characteristics raised simulated users' attribution to the assistant. We found that relational needs such as attachment anxiety raised it as theory predicts, some general personality traits raised it as well, and AI-specific characteristics the least. By contrast, the assistant's social style barely changed simulated users' mind attribution. Instead, sycophantic instructions raised the assistant's attribution to itself. Memory raised users' attribution only with some user models. The model playing the user changed overall attribution and the effects of characteristics, style, and memory. Our framework measures how persona descriptions affect mind attribution in simulation. It gives concrete hypotheses for human studies and shows the need for more consistent user simulators.

papers.title: Chiral Domain-Wall Modes in Topological Adaptive Quantum Dynamics
papers.abstract: Quantum dynamical systems driven by both unitary evolution and measurements open a new landscape of nonequilibrium phases of matter. The role of topology in enriching this landscape remains less understood than that of entanglement and symmetry. A particularly interesting question concerns protected dynamical modes localized on spacetime domain walls between topologically distinct dynamical phases. These dynamical topological domain-wall modes (DTDMs) are well understood only for $0+1$D walls in $1+1$D fermionic dynamics. In this work, we study $1+1$D topological domain walls in $2+1$D charge-conserving free-fermion dynamics, modeled by topological adaptive circuits that steer the two sides of each wall toward a Chern insulator and a trivial insulator through measurements and feedforward corrections. Although the circuits target no particular wall state, each wall hosts $1+1$D chiral DTDMs. At long times in each quantum trajectory, they exhibit logarithmic scaling of entanglement and charge variance and algebraically decaying density correlations, surprisingly consistent with the ground state of a $1+1$D chiral free-fermion conformal field theory. This contrasts with purely $1+1$D charge-conserving free-fermion dynamics, which exhibits only area-law entanglement at finite measurement rates. We also show that the chiral DTDMs exhibit slow purification dynamics. When the system starts from a maximally mixed state, the DTDMs' entropy decays algebraically, accompanied by a vanishing Lyapunov gap, whereas each domain purifies on an $\mathcal{O}(1)$ timescale. Finally, we propose a physical picture for the long-time behavior of the DTDMs by treating the adaptive circuit model as a quantum cooling algorithm. Our results show that topological phases of adaptive dynamics can protect chiral modes on spacetime domain walls against repeated wavefunction collapse and Born-rule randomness.

papers.title: A Quantile-Based Framework for Bimodal Distribution Construction
papers.abstract: This study suggests a novel quantile-based framework to construct bimodal distribution which does not rely on mixture representations or closed-form probability density functions. This proposed approach induces bimodality by transforming the quantile density through a strictly positive modulation function so that it can preserve the support and tail behavior of a chosen baseline distribution with providing explicit control over modal structure. The method is shown to apply broadly across bounded, semi-bounded and unbounded distribution families which include power, reflected power, logistic, Weibull and generalized lambda distributions. Simulation studies and a real-data application were performed which have shown that the proposed construction yields smooth, interpretable and computationally stable bimodal models and it also provides a flexible alternative to classical mixture-based approaches. Also this framework allows gradual transitions between unimodal and bimodal shapes which make it well suited for modeling overlapping regimes which are commonly encountered in real-world data. This proposed methodology therefor offers a robust and interpretable tool for bimodal modeling without requiring latent class assumptions or complex estimation procedures.

papers.title: Horseshoe-Type Shrinkage from Ratio-Generated Priors
papers.abstract: We develop a class of horseshoe-type shrinkage priors generated by ratios of independent numerator and denominator random variables. Large denominator values produce concentration near zero, small denominator values generate heavy tails, and the numerator determines scale and geometry and may also influence tail behavior. We establish general origin and tail asymptotics, including power and logarithmic singularities. Under a Gaussian likelihood and regularly varying prior tails, the posterior mean approaches the observation for large signals, with risk approaching that of the unshrunk observation. The denominator also induces a latent shrinkage factor. For a Cauchy denominator, this factor has exactly the ${\rm Beta}(1/2,1/2)$ distribution, whatever the numerator. With a Gaussian numerator and appropriate scale calibration, it recovers the classical horseshoe shrinkage coefficient, whereas non-Gaussian numerators can change the effective posterior shrinkage, even in its asymptotic rate. The Cauchy/Cauchy prior illustrates the theory, with a logarithmic singularity at the origin in one dimension, power singularities in higher dimensions, and logarithmically modified Cauchy-order tails. Its posterior mean shrinks smoothly, whereas its spatial median behaves nearly as a threshold rule. We also compare the Cauchy/Cauchy posterior mean with fifteen established shrinkage procedures on the four standard Donoho-Johnstone test functions, finding competitive, though not uniformly superior, wavelet-denoising performance. The ratio construction generalizes several published shrinkage priors and offers a flexible framework for sparse estimation, with natural applications to wavelet shrinkage, variable selection, and structured multivariate shrinkage.

papers.title: Do Not Let the Prior Heal the Anomaly: Selective Anchoring for Detection from Incomplete Measurements
papers.abstract: Generative priors can recover anatomical detail from incomplete medical measurements, but may erase the very lesions that imaging aims to detect, even when the measurements contain evidence of them. We introduce selective anchoring that protects reliably measured image components from prior-driven changes, while allowing expressive generative models to reconstruct unresolved structure. Acquisition uncertainty in the protected components is either added deterministically to the downstream test or carried by the ensemble through stochastic perturbations of the readings. We implement this principle as a wrapper for pretrained diffusion and flow samplers and as AnchoredFM, a fast constrained flow model. Under a linear-Gaussian measurement model, the protected coefficients are unbiased in expectation and achieve nominal interval coverage across repeated acquisitions, independently of the learned prior. Across sparse-view CT, accelerated brain MRI, and photoacoustic tomography, selective anchoring improves lesion contrast preservation and uncertainty reliability, and can reduce reconstruction error within lesions. For tumor detection in accelerated MRI, with a healthy reference estimated from the measurements alone, deterministic anchoring raises mean AUROC across eight samplers from 78.4% to 84.6% and lesion sensitivity at 0.25 false-positive marks per slice from 38.8% to 47.5%, with gains in all four predefined tumor-size groups. At thresholds frozen on healthy validation data, mean sensitivity rises from 20.2% to 44.1% (37.6% with stochastic anchoring). These findings show how expressive generative priors can reconstruct unresolved anatomy without healing away the abnormalities that the measurements support.

papers.title: Online Prediction System for Proactive Autoscaling
papers.abstract: We present an online learning system for short-term time series forecasting that enables proactive autoscaling in large-scale distributed systems. Unlike traditional forecasting methods that focus on modeling seasonality and long-term trends, the system targets high-accuracy, low-latency predictions for immediate future intervals for dynamic resource management in internet-scale infrastructures. The system employs a two-stage architecture: a seasonality decomposition stage followed by a residual correction stage using lightweight linear models with engineered features. By retraining models on-the-fly for every prediction cycle, the online prediction system continuously adapts to changing demand patterns without requiring persistent model storage or feature drift monitoring. Deployed across many heterogeneous services, the system processes over 900K predictions per hour; in an offline evaluation on production traffic, its STL-based configuration reduces prediction error (MAPE) by 18.6\% relative to the previous production model. In production, the system has saved an estimated 118K servers daily.

papers.title: A Hierarchy of Risk Certificates for Representation-Based Prediction
papers.abstract: Representation-based prediction underlies many machine-learning systems. Yet a fitted predictor's failure to meet an accuracy requirement does not establish that its representation-decoder class cannot meet it. We study optimal population mean squared error (MSE) over Lipschitz decoders acting on a fixed representation. For blocks of $b\geq2$ independent and identically distributed (iid) observations, we minimize total squared error (normalized by $b-1$) under pairwise Lipschitz constraints. We prove that expected block scores form nondecreasing lower bounds on optimal class risk and converge to that risk on compact metric feature spaces, although no fixed block size provides a uniform relative guarantee. Verified dual lower bounds and iid calibration observations independent of model development, with bounded targets and predictions, yield simultaneous lower confidence bounds on optimal class risk and upper confidence bounds on fitted-predictor risk. These bounds can establish that every admissible decoder exceeds a prescribed MSE threshold or that an admissible fitted predictor meets it. Controlled experiments illustrate population-risk certification; fixed PTB-XL and Bike Sharing experiments provide deterministic empirical-risk conclusions. The results support principled assessment and selection of representation-decoder configurations. Efficient certification at scale and extensions to dependent observations remain open problems.

papers.title: Acoustic Priors from the Latest Cosmic Microwave Background Data
papers.abstract: We revisit the physics of the acoustic peaks and illustrate how early-Universe information in the cosmic microwave background (CMB) can be disentangled from late-time signatures imprinted by gravitational lensing and the integrated Sachs-Wolfe (ISW) effect. Applying this separation to Planck PR4, ACT DR6, and SPT-3G D1 temperature and polarization data combined with the joint lensing reconstruction, we update the model-independent constraints on the angular acoustic scale and the physical densities, $100θ_*=1.04100\pm0.00021$, $ω_{\rm b}=(2.2440\pm0.0099)\times10^{-2}$, and $ω_{\rm bc}=0.1410\pm0.0011$. These constraints are consistent with the previous Planck PR4-only analysis and remain stable for extended late-time cosmologies beyond $Λ$CDM. Adding ACT DR6 to the combination favors a higher $ω_{\rm b}$ and, through their correlation, a higher primordial tilt $n_{\rm s}$ than PR4 alone. The reconstructed lensing spectrum exceeds that of $Λ$CDM, with two features near $L\simeq50$ and $L\sim10^3$, and the excess is reduced when WMAP replaces the Planck primary spectra. Marginalizing over the lensing-induced peak smoothing, rather than tying it to the late-time model, lowers the preference of the CMB and DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) for $w_0w_a$CDM over $Λ$CDM from $3.0σ$ to $1.9σ$, or from $3.2σ$ to $2.4σ$ when Union3.1 supernovae are added. We further use the acoustic prior to predict BAO distances from CMB data alone under several late-time expansion histories, testing their consistency with DESI measurements assuming standard pre-recombination physics.

papers.title: FlowersBench: A FluidFlower-Inspired Dataset for Benchmarking Carbon Storage Surrogates Across Geological Structures
papers.abstract: Machine learning surrogates are emerging as a computationally efficient tool for uncertainty quantification in geological carbon storage (GCS). Geological structure constitutes a major source of uncertainty; however, existing benchmark simulation datasets predominantly vary petrophysical and operational parameters within a fixed geological setting. Generalisation to unseen geological structures therefore remains largely unexplored. We introduce FlowersBench, a benchmark dataset of 5,000 two-dimensional, reservoir-scale CO$_2$ storage simulations across 244 structural geometries. The geometries are sampled from an in-house structural generator inspired by the FluidFlower experiments and Case B of the 11th Society of Petroleum Engineers Comparative Solution Project (SPE11B). Each simulation is run with Open Porous Media (OPM) Flow over a 50-year injection period and a 500-year post-injection monitoring period. Test geometries are withheld from training to assess generalisation to unseen structural geometries. Two additional subsets support evaluation under structural shift. The first extends the parameter ranges of the structural generator beyond those used for training, and the second introduces an unseen topology of multiple parallel faults. A baseline U-Net surrogate is trained to predict CO$_2$ gas saturation. In representative test cases, the surrogate recovers the main migration pathways, including lateral spreading beneath low-permeability layers and upward flow along fault damage zones, with errors concentrated near the plume boundary. Under both structural shifts, prediction error exceeds that on the held-out geometries, and the increase in relative error is greater for the unseen fault topology. FlowersBench is publicly available and provides a common basis for evaluating GCS surrogates across geological structures.

papers.title: Addressing Missing Exposures in Causal Inference: A Practical Guide
papers.abstract: Missing exposure data are a common challenge in epidemiologic studies that can complicate the identification and estimation of causal effects. Particularly for researchers constructing doubly-robust estimators, it can be unclear how to adapt standard methods such as augmented inverse probability weighting (AIPW) to account for missing exposures. This paper clarifies challenges posed by missing exposures, and discusses approaches available for doubly-robust estimation in these settings. We outline numerous mechanisms that can give rise to missing exposures in practice, and demonstrate why double-robustness alone does not protect complete-case AIPW from missing exposure bias. We highlight three broad approaches for addressing this bias: multiply-robust estimation, single imputation and multiple imputation. Using complete-data AIPW---the estimator one would construct in the absence of missing data---as a benchmark, we demonstrate how these approaches impute different components of the ideal complete-data estimator. We discuss practical implementation challenges, including whether outcome information should be used to impute exposures or predict exposure missingness. Through simulations, we illustrate the critical roles of the missingness mechanism, treatment effect heterogeneity and model specification on the performance of these approaches. We conclude with recommendations to help researchers choose an analysis strategy and inform modeling choices involved in their implementation.

papers.title: Using a static spacetime subsystem code to calculate Floquet code distance
papers.abstract: Dynamical codes, including Floquet codes, can capture time-dependent phenomena in quantum error correction circuits that are absent from static stabilizer or subsystem codes, such as detecting regions and error propagation. They are also capable of preserving more logical qubits than corresponding schemes in which the same syndrome-extraction measurements are performed without being distributed over time. However, evaluating the performance of dynamical codes is more complicated than for static codes because error detection depends on when an error occurs within the measurement schedule. In this work, we introduce a mapping from the measurement sequence of a Floquet code to a static spacetime subsystem code and show that calculating the distance of a Floquet code can be reduced to calculating the distance of the corresponding static subsystem code. Crucially, our mapping preserves code distance, a property that is not guaranteed for general spacetime code mappings. This reduction converts the dynamical distance problem into a static subsystem code problem, substantially simplifying the analysis of Floquet measurement schedules and facilitating the evaluation of fault tolerance for new measurement schemes.

papers.title: On the binding and stability of CeO2 molecules on low-index Au surfaces
papers.abstract: Many multi-phase thin films grown by self-assembly involve co-deposition of both metallic and oxide phases that grow into the same film. Under such conditions, the oxide species may be present in stoichiometric molecular form on the surface of the metallic phase. Quantifying the stability, binding, and diffusion of such molecular oxide states on metallic surfaces is critical for understanding self-assembly. In this work, we investigate the binding and stability of CeO2 molecules on Au surfaces using spin-polarized density functional theory calculations. Specifically, we examine how the configuration of the CeO2 molecule, its binding energy and binding free energy, structural stability, effective charge, and projected electronic density of states vary among various binding sites on Au(001), Au(110), and Au(111) surfaces. Molecular CeO2 was found to be more favorable on all Au surfaces than its atomic constituents. It was also found that the bent CeO2 molecule configuration is more stable than the linear counterpart, with the Ce atom on the hollow site and the O atoms on the top sites. In addition, the configurations of the CeO2 molecule on Au surfaces with a binding energy around or weaker than -1 eV were found to have a low probability of existence above room temperature. Furthermore, the charge transfer was found to occur in such a way that the CeO2 molecule becomes polarized on all surfaces, but the polarization is stronger only for the strongly bonded states on Au(001) and Au(110) surfaces. Finally, three different cases of how the CeO2 molecule binds to Au(001), Au(110), and Au(111) were identified: case 1: chemisorption with symmetric bonds, case 2: chemisorption with asymmetric bonds, and case 3: physisorption with symmetric bonds. These three cases of CeO2 binding are present on Au(001) and Au(110), but only cases 2 and 3 occur on Au(111).

papers.title: Temporal Weight Surgery: Repairing Video Grounding with LLM Editors
papers.abstract: A surgeon first finds what is wrong, then fixes only that part. We use this idea for video grounding, where video-language models often find the right moment in a long video but write its time wrong. In Temporal Weight Surgery (TWS), a general-purpose LLM reads the model's weights and activations, finds where the error arises and repairs it there, without gradients. Separate sessions find the same cause, and this diagnosis of where and why the model fails is our main contribution. Three GPT-6 Astra sessions trace a dropped digit in TimeLens-8B to one MLP layer, and the largest edit gains 7.9 mIoU on 1,215 unseen questions and 18.3 on videos of 30 minutes or more. Two Claude Opus 5.5 sessions trace minutes written as seconds in Qwen3-VL-8B to the separator and gain 2.9 and 1.3. Before any edit, its answers often have the right minute and the wrong separator, and fixing only the separator lifts their mIoU from 13.1 to 19.2. Every improving edit beats a random edit of its size, and the edited models run as fast as before.

papers.title: Quantum Copy Complexity of Testing Monotonicity and Other Properties
papers.abstract: We study the sample complexity of testing monotonicity of Boolean functions when the tester is given only copies of the quantum function state $|ψ_f\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}|x,f(x)\rangle$. We give a tester with sample complexity $O\left(\min\left\{\frac{n}{\varepsilon^3}, \frac{n^{3/2}}{\varepsilon^2}\right\}\right)$, improving on the previous $\widetilde O(n^2/\varepsilon^2)$ upper bound of [CNS26]. We also prove the first nontrivial lower bounds for monotonicity testing from quantum function states, matching our upper bounds over a broad range of $\varepsilon$. Our upper bounds use two approaches. The first approach refines the Fourier-based tester of [CNS26] by handling high-influence functions separately, adapting an idea from [KMS18]. The second approach uses the classical path tester of [KMS18] by constructing a quantum observable whose expectation equals the path tester's violation probability. To prove the lower bounds, we place independent functions in mutually incomparable regions of the Boolean hypercube, building on the classical constructions of [BB16, CWX17]. We introduce a new argument for the quantum setting that replaces a fixed number of copies with a Poisson-distributed number of copies, allowing the contributions from different regions to be analyzed independently. This same framework also allows us to prove an $Ω(n^2)$ lower bound for testing union-closedness and $2$-monotonicity from quantum function states.

papers.title: Escape Time with Quenched Extrinsic Fluctuations in Positive Feedback Systems
papers.abstract: Gene regulatory networks with positive feedback often exhibit multiple stable steady states representing distinct cellular phenotypes, allowing stochastic fluctuations to drive phenotypic switching between basins of attraction. Such transitions are commonly characterized by escape-time statistics. While previous studies have typically analyzed intrinsic fluctuation or dynamical environmental fluctuation separately, the combined effect of intrinsic biochemical fluctuation and quenched (slowly varying) extrinsic cell-to-cell parameter heterogeneity on population-level switching dynamics remains less understood. In this study, we formulate a theoretical framework to compute escape-time moments by combining the backward chemical Fokker--Planck equation with population averaging over a stationary distribution of kinetic parameters. We apply this approach to two paradigmatic bistable motifs---positive autoregulation and the genetic Toggle Switch---and quantify how quenched extrinsic heterogeneity modifies switching times across a population of autonomous cells. Our results show that extrinsic parameter variability can substantially alter the mean switching time and, more prominently, increase its dispersion, producing highly heterogeneous switching kinetics across genetically identical cells. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for cell-to-cell parameter heterogeneity when characterizing stochastic phenotypic switching in biological populations.

papers.title: Pohozaev identity, nonexistence and existence for mixed local-nonlocal $(p,q)$-Laplacian
papers.abstract: We study the mixed local-nonlocal operator $\mathcal{L}_{p,q}=-Δ_p+(-Δ)^s_q$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$. First, we prove a Pohozaev identity for bounded, continuous weak solutions of $\mathcal{L}_{p,q} u=f(u)$, where $f$ is any continuous function. We impose no growth condition on $f$. Combined with the Nehari identity, this gives nonexistence of nontrivial solutions for nonlinearities that are supercritical, or subcritical, with respect to both operators. For $f(t)=|t|^{r-2}t$, this rules out all $r$ outside the interval between $p^*$ and $q^*_s$. Second, we show that this interval is exactly where solutions exist. When $p^*\neq q^*_s$ and $r \in \left(\min\{p^*,q^*_s\}, \;\max\{p^*,q^*_s\}\right)$, we obtain a nonnegative radial solution by constrained minimization and a ground state by using the Pohozaev identity as a constraint. Finally, we show that the two solutions have the same energy.

papers.title: On the Structure Constants of ${\cal N}=2$ Liouville Theory
papers.abstract: We show the structure constants of $\mathcal{N}=2$ spacelike Liouville theory. The absence of self-duality under $b\leftrightarrow b^{-1}$, where $b$ is the Liouville coupling, prevents a straightforward application of the standard bootstrap methods used in $\mathcal{N}=0$ and $\mathcal{N}=1$ Liouville theory. Motivated by the fermionic FZZ duality with the $SL(2,\mathbb{R})/U(1)$ supercoset theory, we establish an algebraic correspondence between the two theories, including a matching of their null vectors. We then derive the three-point structure constants in superspace. The neutral sector structure constants are associated with the spectral-flow-preserving structure constant of the $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ WZW model, while the two charged sectors correspond to its spectral-flow-violating structure constants. Finally, we give the correct relative normalization between the neutral and charged sectors and test crossing symmetry numerically.

papers.title: LGCount: Layout-Guided Diffusion for Zero-Shot Object Counting
papers.abstract: Class-agnostic counting requires the user to specify what to count, usually with a class name or a few annotated boxes. We propose a richer text-based specification: a structured layout that names the target, the region that holds it, the distractors to ignore. A prompt upsampler writes this layout from the image and the requested category alone, and an image-editing diffusion model, adapted into a single-step counter, turns it into a density map. Because counting datasets pair each image with a single valid density map, a counter trained on it learns to ignore the layout. We therefore train on synthetic counterfactuals in which one image admits several valid density maps, so that the layout cannot be ignored. On FSC-147 we improve on the previous zero-shot state of the art and we set the best reported result on LOOKALIKES while being told the least about each image. A single photograph can be counted by category, by region, or by granularity without retraining.

papers.title: A Sequent Calculus for the Quantified Reflection Calculus $\mathrm{QRC}_1$: Cut-Elimination, Interpolation, and NP-Completeness
papers.abstract: We introduce $\mathrm{G3QRC}_1$, the first Gentzen-style sequent calculus for Borges and Joosten's Quantified Reflection Calculus ($\mathrm{QRC}_1$). As a strictly positive, first-order modal logic, $\mathrm{QRC}_1$ crucially escapes Vardanyan's $Π^0_2$-completeness theorem for quantified provability logic, while remaining arithmetically complete with respect to Peano and Heyting Arithmetic. The central innovation of $\mathrm{G3QRC}_1$ is a pair of context-erasing modal rules that simultaneously account for the monotonicity and transitivity axioms by deliberately discarding parametric context across modal boundaries. This structural bottleneck allows for a clean proof of cut-admissibility via a standard lexicographic induction, circumventing the complex loop-checking typically required for provability logics. Cut admissibility yields an instantiated subformula property and supports a direct canonical proof of the finite model property. We streamline the adequate Kripke semantics by interpreting constants globally. We also establish a split-context Craig interpolation theorem and a contextual form of left uniform interpolation, uniformly eliminating private predicate symbols, constants, and free parameters. Finally, by leveraging the rigid structural constraints of the context-erasing rules and the absence of left-branching connectives, we prove that, over the standard fixed countable signatures specified in the paper, the decision problem for $\mathrm{QRC}_1$ is $\mathbf{NP}$-complete, situating this quantified modal logic in a comparatively low nondeterministic complexity class.

papers.title: NEVA: Natural-Language Co-Evolution and Validation of Microarchitectures
papers.abstract: Recent large language model (LLM)-guided evolutionary approaches have demonstrated the potential to automate microarchitectural design exploration. However, existing approaches primarily evolve C++ simulator code rather than reasoning directly about the microarchitectural designs it represents. As C++ code embodies hardware designs with several layers of abstraction, evolving it directly forces LLMs to reason through implementation details rather than the actual architectural mechanisms, hardware state, and decision rules that define a microarchitectural design. To this end, we propose NEVA, an LLM-guided methodology that generates new microarchitectural policies by extracting, integrating and adapting architectural concepts from published research. NEVA extracts the underlying concepts from prior works into a structured knowledge library, which then guides the evolution of joint natural-language architectural specifications. This approach addresses three key challenges: architectural representation in natural language, validation of candidate designs under hardware constraints, and the coordination of microarchitecture components using diagnostic feedback through co-evolution. We evaluate NEVA across single-core and multicore configurations using SPEC CPU2017/2026, Google, GAP, and XSBench workloads, and compare specification-level evolution against code-level evolution across different search strategies. Under Claude Opus 5.5, NEVA discovers designs achieving up to 4.8% higher held-out single-core performance than the Pythia-Mockingjay baseline. A selected EvoX design achieves improvements of 3.4% and 1.5% under full and restricted memory bandwidth, respectively, although its multicore performance does not differ significantly from the baseline. The EvoX search evaluates 40 candidates over 2.2 days, with approximately $320 in LLM usage at API list prices.

papers.title: Error estimates for a structure-preserving finite-element scheme of quasi-incompressible Navier-Stokes-Maxwell-Stefan systems
papers.abstract: A conforming finite-element scheme for quasi-incompressible Navier-Stokes-Maxwell-Stefan systems in a bounded domain with periodic boundary conditions is presented. The system consists of the Navier-Stokes equations, together with a quasi-incompressibility constraint, coupled with the cross-diffusion Maxwell--Stefan equations. The numerical scheme preserves the partial masses and the quasi-incompressibility constraint and dissipates the discrete energy. First-order error estimates in space and time are shown for a diffusion-augmented mobility matrix by using the relative energy method and suitable projection error estimates. Numerical experiments in two space dimensions illustrate the convergence of the scheme and indicate second-order convergence in space in the $L^2$ norm.

papers.title: Anomalous scaling of coalescence in a Hele-Shaw cell
papers.abstract: We investigate the merging of two drops between two narrowly spaced plates, a so-called Hele-Shaw cell. For this, we solve the Hele-Shaw equations in two dimensions, driven by surface tension, focusing on early times after initial reconnection. Combining numerical simulations with theory, we show that the coalescence dynamics are self-similar at early times, with the size of the contact region between the drops growing as $t^{3/13}$. We find this power law using a matched asymptotic analysis, which reveals a complex geometry consisting of a small bubble that gets entrained between the drops as they come together. These predictions match perfectly to our simulations, and agree with the most recent experimental data.

papers.title: Stark units and cyclotomic Iwasawa theory over complex cubic fields
papers.abstract: For cyclotomic extensions of complex cubic fields, we prove the integral rank-$1$ and rational rank-$2$ abelian Stark conjectures. More generally, we prove a relative theorem on the higher-rank Rubin--Stark conjectures for cubic extensions of number fields. We then apply our Stark unit constructions to the Bergeron--Charollois--García conjectures on elliptic gamma values. Finally, we prove an Iwasawa main conjecture relating norm-compatible systems of Stark units to ideal class groups in cyclotomic towers over complex cubic fields.

papers.title: Geodesic Causal Forests: Learning Heterogeneous Treatment Effects for Random Objects
papers.abstract: Causal forests and orthogonal learners estimate heterogeneous treatment effects for scalar or Euclidean outcomes, yet outcomes are increasingly random objects, such as compositions, covariance matrices, distributions, or networks, in metric spaces without linear structure. We introduce geodesic causal forests for conditional geodesic treatment effects. Geodesic transport moves each geodesic between conditional Fréchet means of the potential outcomes to a common reference, making effects comparable across individuals. Because random objects cannot be added or subtracted, Euclidean residual corrections are unavailable; we instead correct the squared-distance loss through which the forest selects splits and estimates effects. The loss is real-valued for every candidate effect, so the correction requires only Fréchet means and leaves second-order nuisance error; for Euclidean outcomes, it recovers doubly robust learning. We establish consistency, convergence rates, and split-selection guarantees under conditions verified for curved and nonsmooth spaces. In simulations with covariance-matrix outcomes, the correction substantially reduces estimation error. For women's livelihood compositions in BRAC's randomized antipoverty program in Bangladesh, new livestock work mainly replaces casual wage work; after alignment, a single effect reproduces much of the variation in percentage-point changes across baseline activities, and the fitted effects are largest among former domestic workers and older women.

papers.title: Understanding Failure Patterns in LLM-Based Mathematical Optimization Modeling
papers.abstract: Industrial optimization involves complex constraints, making optimization modeling difficult to automate. Large language models (LLMs) have been explored for generating optimization models from natural language, but their reliability in end-to-end settings remains limited, often producing non-executable, infeasible, or feasible but incorrect solutions. In this work, we study failure modes in LLM-based optimization modeling by decomposing the process into three components: mathematical reasoning, solver usage, and domain knowledge, and constructing datasets that target each aspect. Using these datasets, we analyze how different components relate to errors and find that they are associated with different types of failure, although these relationships are not always strong or consistent. Furthermore, while combining these components improves execution reliability, feasible but incorrect solutions remain the dominant failure mode, suggesting a remaining gap between executability and correctness. These findings highlight limitations of current dataset designs and suggest the importance of data that better capture constraint completeness and formulation accuracy to enhance reliability.

papers.title: Why Does Sensor Depth Fail Learned Manipulation Policies? Finding the Failure Mode with ACT
papers.abstract: Learned manipulation policies, from task-specific imitation policies to vision-language-action (VLA) models, rely primarily on RGB images. While some studies report gains from sensor depth, others avoid depth cameras because of measurement noise. Depth cameras introduce both noise and missing depth values (holes), whose relative effects remain unclear. In this study, we calibrate a sensor model using a real wrist-mounted stereo camera and separately evaluate noise and holes on RGB-D imitation policies with three visual encoders in simulation. We found that complete depth improves success by approximately ten percentage points, and most of this gain persists even at twenty times the camera's noise level. In contrast, holes covering about one-sixth of the wrist image eliminate the detectable benefit of depth. The validity mask strongly influences depth reliance: marking a small fraction of pixels as invalid reduces reliance, while filling holes and marking them valid restores most of the benefit. Policies trained on clean depth also lose performance when holes appear only at deployment, sometimes falling below RGB-only performance. These findings suggest that depth cameras for learned policies should therefore be judged by depth coverage more than measurement precision.

papers.title: The Marauder's Map: Bézier Manifolds Reveal Hidden Surfaces for Model Merging and Ensembling
papers.abstract: Neural circuits are famously more robust than deep networks. This is often explained through degeneracy, where structurally distinct configurations support the same function. However, real biological systems exhibit a more flexible form of degeneracy in which specialized circuits continually adapt towards new competencies through localized changes while preserving existing function. Deep learning studies degeneracy through mode connectivity, which connects same-task networks by low-loss curves, sheets, or volumes. However, the field lacks a counterpart to flexible degeneracy, which demands more than ordinary mode connectivity. Defining such an analogue requires asking whether many independently initialized models trained on distinct tasks can be connected by a high-dimensional region of multi-task solutions. We introduce $\textit{Nimbus}$, which learns a high-dimensional Bézier manifold connecting $N$ specialists, going beyond the one-dimensional paths and two-dimensional sheets of mode connectivity work. A naive parameterization would scale combinatorially with $N$, but $\textit{Nimbus}$ requires learning corrections of only 3 interaction orders, showing that the connecting manifold has surprisingly low complexity yet supports multi-task competencies. The resulting manifold forms a navigable "Marauder's Map" that connects specialist models through a shared geometry of competent solutions. Trained across vision and language domains, $\textit{Nimbus}$ produces manifolds that are functionally and locally weight-flat: ensembles sampled from them degrade more gracefully than baselines under input and weight perturbations, with the largest gains in NLL loss and calibration error. $\textit{Nimbus}$ supplies a deep learning interpretation of flexible degeneracy, recasting model connectivity from a low-dimensional path between distant solutions into a high-dimensional volume of nearby ones.

papers.title: Identifying Renormalization Group Interfaces of Massless WZW Flows $\widehat{\mathfrak{su}}(2)_k \to \widehat{\mathfrak{su}}(2)_1$
papers.abstract: A renormalization-group interface encodes how a flow relates operators at short and long distances. We identify this interface up to topological dressing for the conjectured massless $\widehat{\mathfrak{su}}(2)_k \to \widehat{\mathfrak{su}}(2)_1$ Wess-Zumino-Witten flows at every odd level $k\geq 3$. Global $SU(2)$ symmetry requires the interface to preserve a diagonal current algebra at level $k+1$, built from the currents on its two sides. The $\mathbb{Z}_2$ center symmetry then selects which representation labels the interface. This identification predicts distinct patterns of low-lying interface excitations for flows to the same infrared fixed point. Spin-chain calculations reproduce these patterns for $k=3$ and $5$, providing independent evidence for both conjectured flows.

papers.title: Graphs with the largest chainable index and their properties
papers.abstract: This paper provides a complete characterization of the set of graphs with the largest chainable index. In particular, it is shown that the number of arcs and vertex degrees of such graphs satisfy strong restrictions. Moreover, graphs with the largest chainable index form five parametric families, and exactly one of them consists of graphs that are not strongly connected. As a consequence, the number of graphs on $n$ vertices with the largest chainable index is computed, and the values of the primitive exponent for these graphs are calculated.

papers.title: Approximate Counting and the Provability of Combinatorial Principles
papers.abstract: Understanding which axioms suffice for the provability of known results in algorithms and complexity and whether they can settle longstanding conjectures in these areas is a fundamental direction at the intersection of logic and computer science. Motivated by this research program and its applications, we investigate bounded arithmetic theories designed to serve as a logical foundation for *probabilistic reasoning*, the relation between these theories, and whether they can prove more theorems than their underlying base theory for *deterministic reasoning*. In more detail, for nearly twenty years, Jeřábek's theory $\mathsf{APC}_1$ [Jeř07a] has provided a standard framework for the formalization of results from theoretical computer science relying on probabilistic techniques. In a recent work, [CLOW26] introduced a (possibly weaker) theory called $\mathsf{APX}_1$. This theory is able to capture a large set of probabilistic arguments using four simple axioms for *approximate counting*. Both theories extend Cook's theory $\mathsf{PV}_1$ [Coo75] for deterministic polynomial-time reasoning. Our main result establishes that, in the relativized setting, $\mathsf{APX}_1$ does not prove the retraction weak pigeonhole principle ($\mathsf{rwPHP}$). Consequently, $\mathsf{APC}_1$ is not conservative over $\mathsf{APX}_1$ with respect to relativized $\forallΣ^b_1$ sentences. Moreover, we establish that the unprovability of $\mathsf{rwPHP}$ is part of a more general phenomenon: for a large class of finite combinatorial principles, the existence of an *infinite model* of the negation of the principle *characterizes* its unprovability in $\mathsf{APX}_1$. This result, which is analogous to a theorem of Riis [Rii94], implies that $\mathsf{PV}_1$ and $\mathsf{APX}_1$ prove exactly the same finite combinatorial principles of this form.

papers.title: Butterfly Effect in Kinetic Plasma Turbulence
papers.abstract: The butterfly effect is a fundamental process in chaotic systems, but it has not previously been characterized in detail for a collisionless turbulent plasma. In this work, we apply particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations of driven turbulence to study the emergence of the butterfly effect from a small initial perturbation to the simulated particles. In particular, we compare pairs of (baseline and perturbed) simulations that differ only by a localized initial perturbation (down to the single-particle level).
